name: Tabitha Lockhart
languages: Spanish (a coach-road Spanish, mostly about horses)
equipment: Leather duster, oiled canvas, with the Southwestern Express Company's brass badge on the lapel
Coach gun (a short double 12-gauge, the company's), loaded
Army revolver (Colt single-action, .45), 6 rounds loaded, worn butt-forward on the left for a cross draw
A spare loaded cylinder for the revolver, in a pouch (Fast Hands)
The messenger's copy of the waybill for the Plata Vieja payroll, with the Bank of the Rio Abajo's serial-number schedule pinned to it, in an oilcloth wallet inside her shirt
The express box key on a chain round her neck, which is now the key to nothing
Lon Brisbane's little Bible, which he left on her seat at the Puerco station
Driving gloves, a slicker and a hat with a stampede string
features: Hard Country (Frontier-Born origin: advantage on saving throws against exhaustion from heat, cold, thirst and hard travel; needs half the usual water one day in three; once per long rest shrugs off a level of trail exhaustion; packs rations that last half again as long)

Quick Draw (Gunslinger: advantage on initiative rolls and on the draw in a showdown; when she rolls initiative and isn't surprised she draws a Sidearm as part of the roll, and drawing or holstering a Sidearm never costs her an interaction)
Gun Hand: Fast Hands (Gunslinger: reloads a revolver as a bonus action, two rounds, and swaps a spare cylinder as a bonus action; this does not change the attack bonus or damage on her sheet)
Fan the Hammer (Gunslinger, 2nd level: fans up to 4 rounds in one action, the first without disadvantage; fanned shots add no ability modifier to damage)

Style: Pistoleer (Gunslinger, 3rd level: when she takes the Attack action with a Sidearm and both shots hit the same creature, it must succeed on a DC 13 WIS save or be frightened of her until the end of its next turn)

The Mail Road (Stage Driver background: knows every station, bad grade and ambush place on the Rio Seco road and the Kansas mail roads; station keepers, hostlers and drivers feed her, change her horses and tell her who rode through; drives any team without a check in ordinary conditions)

personality.traits: I say very little and notice everything. I sit facing the door, I sleep with my boots on, and I count the passengers every time the coach stops. I do not laugh often, and when I do it surprises people.
personality.ideals: A messenger brings the box in. Not most of the time. Every time. That is the whole of the job, and it is the only thing anyone has ever paid me to be the best at.
personality.bonds: Lon Brisbane, my partner for two years, who prayed for me every night on the road whether I wanted him to or not. My mother and sisters in Nicodemus, Kansas, to whom I send half my pay.
personality.flaws: I was inside the coach when Lon was killed, because the company put the senior messenger on the box and the other inside, and he was senior by a month. I will not forgive myself, and I will not forgive whoever planned it, and I am not sure that I can tell justice from the other thing.

appearance: A tall, rangy Black woman of twenty-six with close-cut hair under a flat-brimmed hat, high cheekbones, a long jaw and a very level stare. Oiled duster with the company badge, a man's shirt and waistcoat, riding skirt over trousers, boots. The coach gun is never more than an arm's length from her hand.
backstory: Tabitha Lockhart was born in 1855 in Kentucky, enslaved, and freed at ten, and in 1877 she went west with her mother and sisters and three hundred other families to found the town of Nicodemus on the Kansas plains. Nicodemus was hard country: dugouts, drought, grasshoppers, and no money at all. Tabitha, who could ride and shoot better than any of her brothers-in-law, hired on with a stage line carrying the mail from the railroad at Ellis, first as a hostler and then, when the regular man quit, on the box. In 1879 the Southwestern Express Company took her on as a shotgun messenger for the New Mexico runs, the only woman it has ever hired for the job. It paid her half what it paid Lon Brisbane, and she has never lost a box. She and Lon have ridden the Rio Seco road together for two years. On the last run the company put them both on, because of the size of the payroll: Lon on the box, Tabitha inside with the passengers. She carries the messenger's copy of the waybill, and the express company's rule is that the messenger who loses a box is dismissed. (Suggested employer: the Southwestern Express Company, already; she means to recover the box and find who killed Lon. Hooks: the serial-number schedule in her shirt, which almost nobody knows exists; Lon's debts, which she paid in May; the company's rule.)
